chapter: On the road with Guitar Slim
title: Slim's band members and playing baritone at the Apollo
summary: Ford lists the band, tells how Ellis Marsalis lent him a baritone, and describes Apollo Theater demands and the station wagon.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: That was my 46-year-old song. Who else was in the band with Slam? With Slam, when I got there it was Lloyd Lambert was the manager, leader of the band. Slam was featured at Traction, he was going to Slam's band, but Lloyd Lambert was really the leader, bass player. And Cotton, Lawrence Cotton was playing piano. And Lloyd played bass, Oscar played drums. Oscar Moore. Yeah. He was with Slam before any of them. And Joe Tillman played tenor sax. Gus played alto, Gus Fontenet. And I played baritone. I was in the band, it's a baritone player. I didn't have a baritone. And I had a good friend, Ellis Marcellus, he's still a good friend, and a wonderful musician, the greatest piano player I'll ever know. He was playing baritone sax. He would be playing with us with Joe Jones sometimes. So he lost. I said, in some kind of way he said, I'll lend you the baritone, because I don't want it no more. He stopped playing baritone, I'm about to play the piano. And I was supposed to buy it from him, but he finally gave it to me. And he loaned me a baritone, and I went to play baritone for about two years, so in 56. And I came on Cry to State. We played Apollo Theater. At the time when Apollo Theater, if you couldn't play, you had to play for a show, they'd put another man in there, you wouldn't make a dime. You had to be able to play the theater, to read the show, and you never saw it before. See, they'd come up there with the show, like they do at the film. No, they were doing it. If you couldn't play that show, somebody would come there and take your spot. So, well. How long were you in the road to the slip? About two years. A little bit better. I was all of 56. And all of 55. Now I don't know if I went there in 55 or late 54. Because they, no, it had to be 55, because they had a 55 wagon, 55 Ford wagon. That's how you all would get around? That's right, a wagon. I met them in Macon, Georgia and went on a train. And they had a 55 Ford wagon, and as many as nine of us went on that wagon at times.
